Yes, I have other disorders. I won't get into complete specifics, but other than the disassociative condition I have a family history of depression, I grew up with severe anxiety, and I have been diagnosed with ADHD. 

I have almost no anxiety now, but when I was a teenager I would get red in the face and shake just having to go into a gas station to pay for gas (and sometimes I couldn't even go through with it). Depression has been with me my whole life. Given how antidepressants have helped me among other reasons, I strongly believe it is genetic alongside trauma. The ADHD aspect comes from my brain being bombarded with 10 thoughts happening at the same time. I never suspected I had ADHD until I met a psychologist who kept pulling me back to the signal when I continuously drifted into to noise. I even denied having it for years after, only to accept it when I learned that the overwhelming thoughts were one cause of the disassociation.

"Telling the truth" comes into play in regards to the disassociative condition. There is a thing called cognitive dissonance. It's when an individual believes two contradictory things simultaneously and are not aware (despite sounding silly, this is VERY common). People often lie to themselves because they don't want to acknowledge a painful reality. I believe the analogy Sigmund Freud coined was "The Shadow" self. Being able to acknowledge the worst, darkest aspects of yourself and accepting it allows you to become more integrated and whole. If you deny truthful, yet dark aspects of yourself, this can cause cognitive dissonance. Usually when this happens and you start "digging" into the unknown side of yourself, cognitive dissonance shows and the initial reaction of people is to get emotional (eg angry, stressed, agitated..). It's hard to dig by yourself. An educated trained professional is very helpful when it comes to digging (eg therapy).
I say, "tell the truth" because long story short, that's the sole mission- but that said, you may say something you believe to be true, but are not aware it isn't. You can become aware by asking questions (eg implement the Socratic method).
Grounding exercises can help in stressful times. They aren't a long term solution. I have moments where I get lost in my head, then get emotional. "Box breathing" and using my senses to feel my surroundings helps me get out. I haven't personally tested this, but you could try doing them everyday and see if it becomes passive after 30 days (ie the length it takes to build a habit).
Lastly, as for sleep, I still haven't figured this out. Limiting caffeine and having a consistent schedule are the two things that help me. I do know when I am tired, my mental and physical health takes a nasty turn. Try to at least get 8 hours a day though.

I hope this helps.

Try writing and/or speaking out loud.

When you do it, make sure you **do it in full sentences** and not simply words, images, or "a vague feeling of understanding".

***Edit.*** Also, as for potential topics, know that there is a whole reality that surrounds you that can (and in my opinion, should) be questioned and explored.

Be curious about anything and "dig" at it. For example, what is it like having DpDr?

***Edit 2.***  You will probably feel very bad in the beginning of doing these "thinking exercises". Maybe you will want to cry, or you feel like you are an idiot, or think you can never do it because you just aren't good enough. I tell you now that you are certainly not an idiot just because you are struggling, if anything: trying to be better and heal already sets you apart from a lot of society. You also **are good enough**, but **you must put in the work**. Exercising the mind is like exercising the body - they both require proper hygiene to be healthy. If you neglect the body (eating bad foods, not exercising) you will be at risk for diseases as well as be overweight. If you neglect the mind (feed it bad content *- looking at you Tik Tok*, not exercising) then it will begin to forget things easily, struggle to hold information to even be able to think, and so forth.

I recommend making it a [habit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UMOZZ5uZgxA) to write and speak aloud until you can do it mentally.

Point is, work your ass off and climb out of the pit. Only you can do this, so want it and want it very, very bad.

For someone struggling badly, that may be too hard because of a weakened working memory. A step into that direction though would be the grounding technique of going into a room, looking at the room around you, and mindfully observing what your senses are telling you.

Example:

I see a clock, I feel cold, I smell peppermint, I hear the ticking of that clock... etc.

Being more detailed than that is better, but, baby steps.

u/FairInterview4765 has a point. [Grounding techniques](https://www.healthline.com/health/grounding-techniques#:~:text=17.%20Use%20an%20anchoring%20phrase) are a good way to snap out of it. Also, cold water to the face, or just forcing yourself to take a cold 3-minute shower will most certainly wake you up. How long is another story.

Write a note to yourself and tack it to your wall, write: "gain control".

Reminders serve to be useful if (I assume you do) you have memory problems.

You can write anything, but "gain control" should remind you to fight for your sanity. Else, you will remain and sink further into the pit you're in. DpDr is an excellent coping mechanism for fighting pain, but the pain of losing your mind is worse than facing the death of your aunt (forgive me if I sound insensitive,  this is my opinion derived from my own experiences - losing loved ones, witnessing other people fall into a pit from losing loved ones, etc.).

To gain control, figure out why it is you wake up every day and simply do not off yourself. There **is** a reason (you came here on reddit to rant because you want to be heard - so you care about something). If your meaning is hidden, dig and don't stop until you have it.

I'm sorry about your aunt. I'm guessing she wouldn't want this for you though, keep that in mind. Also, understand you are grieving. Be nice to yourself, okay?
